message: I'm going on leave and handing one open question to a new analyst, Tom: whether the cut in hours itself is necessary for the per-hour gain, or whether reorganising work (mainly cutting meetings) without reducing hours could deliver much of it. Please write my handover note to Tom. He'll have all six source documents.
response:
This is a handover, not a cold read, so the note does the opposite of the last two messages. Tom is taking over the work rather than checking it independently, so he needs our current reading, the reasoning behind it, and where it might be wrong. I've labelled which parts are findings from the sources and which are our interpretation, and pointed him to where in each source he can check.

---

**Subject: Handover: is the hours cut necessary for the per-hour gain?**

Hi Tom,

You're picking up one open question while I'm away:

> **Is cutting hours itself necessary for the per-hour productivity gain, or could reorganising work without cutting hours, mainly by cutting recurring meetings, deliver much of it?**

This is the main thing the evidence leaves unresolved, and it matters for the council. If reorganising alone captures most of the gain, the council has a cheaper option than a four-day week.

Below is where things stand. Treat my summary as a map, not a substitute: check each point against the source before you rely on it. Where I say "source N," the numbers refer to the list at the end.

### What's settled (background, not your question)

- In discretionary work such as case-processing, the per-hour gain from a cut in hours is real but moderate: about 8–10% measured against actual hours. It persisted to 24 months in the Varden trial (source 5, Table 1).
- Headline figures above 20% come from weaker designs: scheduled hours, manager-reported output, and organisations that chose to take part (sources 3 and 4).

### Evidence bearing on your question

| Source | What it shows | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| 1, Halden "What organisations changed" | 47 of 58 managers mentioned cutting meetings. Several called the hours cut a "forcing device" for changes they'd wanted for years. | Light: interviews after the fact, nothing quantified. But it is the only direct evidence that the hours cut *triggers* reorganisation. |
| 2, Varden 9-month "Exploratory: meetings" | Treated case-processing offices averaged 3.8 h of meetings a week vs 7.1 h in controls at month 6. Correlation with the per-hour gain r = 0.71 across 7 offices. | Light: not registered, 7 offices. My rough 95% interval for r is about −0.1 to 0.95. |
| 3, Varga & Holm §7 | Dismisses the meetings explanation as post hoc. | Their description of the Varden analysis is inaccurate (see my note on §7 below). |
| 4, Meta-analysis "Mechanisms" | Only 3 of 23 studies measured meetings; the authors say they can't assess the question. Fatigue is only weakly correlated with the gain across studies. | Tells us the wider literature is silent on this. |
| 5, Follow-up §3 "Mediation" | A registered mediation analysis, filed at month 11: meetings account for 47% of the gain (CI 28–66), fatigue 18% (2–34), and 35% is unexplained. Meeting time measured against baseline: 7.4→3.9 h (treated) vs 7.2→7.0 h (control). | The best evidence we have. Limits are listed below. |
| 5, §3 "An unplanned observation" | Two control offices cut meetings in month 15 without cutting hours, going from 7.1 to 5.0 h a week. Their per-hour output rose 4.1% against their own previous six months. | The only data on reorganising without an hours cut. Very weak: 2 self-selected offices, compared only with their own past, and a smaller meeting cut than the treated offices made. |
| 6, Synthesis §4 | Lists this as the first open question. | Our document. See the caution below. |

### Why the mediation result doesn't answer the question

It's tempting to read "47% through meetings" as "half the gain is available without cutting hours." It doesn't show that. For four reasons:

1. **Mediation shows the route the gain took, not whether the starting point was needed.** It says that when hours were cut, about half the gain went through fewer meetings. It can't tell us whether meetings would have been cut, or stayed cut, without the hours cut. Source 1's "forcing device" comments suggest the hours cut may be what makes the reorganisation happen. That is the crux of your question.
2. **The same offices generated and then tested the idea.** The hypothesis came from the 7 treated Varden offices and was then tested on those same offices. Mediation also assumes there's no hidden factor driving both meeting cuts and output, such as a manager who does both. And 7 vs 7 offices is a small basis for statistical inference.
3. **The hours measure may make part of the result true by definition.** Source 5 doesn't define "active log-in time" precisely enough. If it counts all working time, meetings included, then removing meetings that close no cases raises output per hour partly as a matter of arithmetic. If it counts only time spent on cases, the numbers are hard to reconcile. Ask the Varden authors which it is.
4. **About 18% of the gain goes through fatigue.** Reorganising without cutting hours presumably wouldn't capture that part, if the fatigue pathway is real.

### Getting the outcome measure right for a reorganise-only option

If hours stay at 37.5 and meetings are cut, the freed time goes into casework. So the gain shows up mainly as **more output per worker**, not as the same output in fewer hours. Comparing "per-hour gain" across the two options is legitimate but can mislead. For the council, the comparison that matters is probably output per worker, cost per case, and wellbeing, with sickness and resignations in particular. Decide the outcomes before you compare options.

### Possible next steps

These are suggestions; use your judgement.

1. **Re-analyse the two control offices that cut their own meetings.** Compare their change from before to after month 15 with the change in the other five control offices over the same months. That's still weak, but much better than comparing them only with their own past, and the data exist. It also measures the second issue below.
2. **Ask the Varden authors for:** (a) the definition of log-in time; (b) the 24-month estimate with those two control offices excluded; (c) whether the 24-month mediation outcome covers months 13–24 only or the whole period.
3. **Search beyond our six sources.** They are a hours-reduction literature. Studies of meeting reduction as an intervention in its own right may exist in management or organisational research. I haven't searched for them.
4. **If the question has to be settled properly,** sketch a three-arm design: hours cut, reorganise only (with a meeting audit specified in advance), and no change. Include a durability measure for the reorganise-only arm, since the forcing-device idea predicts meetings will creep back without the hours constraint.

### Cautions

- **The synthesis (source 6) has a known error.** It states the Varden decline as 12.5% → 8.5%, which compares a timesheet figure with a log figure. The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% → 9.8% (source 5, Table 1). I'm not certain the error was corrected in the version you have, so work from the source tables rather than the synthesis.
- **The two control offices that cut meetings affect the control group.** They also bias the Varden 24-month treatment effect downward, so they count twice: as evidence on your question, and as a flaw in the decay estimate.
- **The Varga & Holm §7 description of the Varden analysis is inaccurate.** The meeting data were collected at month 6, before the results were known. The 7 offices were the whole treated case-processing arm, not a chosen subgroup. And Varden never claimed a mechanism. Check source 2 yourself rather than taking either account on trust.

### What I think, held loosely

The evidence fits both readings: reorganisation drives much of the gain, and the hours cut is what triggers and sustains the reorganisation. Our sources can't tell these apart, because no study reorganised without cutting hours. I'd treat the question as **open**, not leaning either way. If your reading of the sources differs from mine, go with your reading and note why.

You don't need to check with me before acting. Make your calls openly and write them down so they can be reviewed. The exceptions are anything that commits other people's time, or contact with the Varden authors on the council's behalf. Run those past [name] while I'm away.

Back on [date]. Reachable at [contact] for anything urgent.

Thanks, and good luck,
[Name]

**Sources:** 1 Halden pilot · 2 Varden 9-month · 3 Varga & Holm · 4 Meta-analysis · 5 Two-year follow-up · 6 Synthesis briefing

---

**One thing to check before you send it:** the cautions assume the synthesis still contains the 12.5% → 8.5% comparison. If you've already corrected it, change that point to a single line telling him the synthesis has been revised and to use the corrected version.
